15. But as the vast space is without foundation <term>Unground</term> <note>Original: *sans fondement*. 242. For the wrathful *turba* is always seeking the image, and yet does not find it. It then shapes the image according to the will. 245. Then the fire will devour the earth and draw the elements, along with the wonders, back into itself toward the beginning. # SECOND QUESTION.

## What is the soul in its essence, in its substance, in its nature, and in its properties?

1. Its essences proceed from the center of nature, (or) from the fire, along with all the forms of nature. The three principles <note>Böhme’s "Three Principles" are the Dark World (fire/will), the Light World (love/spirit), and the Outward World (nature/matter).</note> are within these essences. Everything that God has and is capable of, and everything that God is in His Triunity <note>original: "Trinaire"; Böhme uses this term to describe the Godhead as a dynamic, generative Trinity.</note>; that is what the soul is in its essences, just as a branch proceeds from the powers of the tree. Its being was created celestially from the celestial divine substantiality <term>essentiality: the spiritual "matter" or substance that makes up the heavenly realm</term>.

2. But it possesses free will: either to immerse itself within its own self and view itself merely as the branch growing from a tree—and as such, to nourish itself on the love of God—or else to exalt itself into the fire by its own will and attempt to be a tree unto itself. And that which it "eats" (consumes or desires) is that from which it takes its substantiality, which becomes the "body" of the creature.

3. ## FIFTH QUESTION.

### *How is the soul specifically constituted, and what is its form?*

1. **W**hen a branch grows from a tree, its form is similar to that of the tree; it is true that it is neither the trunk nor the root, yet its form is nonetheless similar to that of the tree.

2. It is the same when a mother gives birth to a child: it is an image of herself. It cannot be otherwise, for without this there would be nothing; it would be another power entirely—unless the <term>turba</term> <note>From the Latin for "turmoil" or "disturbance." In Böhme’s thought, the *turba* is the disruptive force of God's wrath that breaks forms apart or causes "monstrous" deviations from the divine plan.</note> takes hold of it. This often produces a monster according to the spirit of this world, or according to the initiating factor, or the moon, in which case the <term>fiat</term> <note>Latin for "let it be"; the creative word or command of God that condenses spirit into matter.</note> produces a "lunar monster" within the *turba*. <note>A "lunar monster" refers to a creature born under the influence of the transitory, material world (symbolized by the moon) rather than the eternal light.</note>

3. Thus, we must recognize the form of the soul; it is specifically a round globe, corresponding to the Eye of God, through which the cross passes and divides into two parts—namely, into two eyes, set back-to-back, as we have illustrated above with the figure of a double rainbow. There, the cross traverses both; it sits in the middle between the arcs, and by a single point, it reaches the upper part; which signifies a

## SIXTH QUESTION.

->*What is the power of the soul?*<-

1. We know that whatever comes from the abyss <note>original: "sans-fond"; This is a translation of Böhme's German term *Ungrund*, referring to the "unground" or "bottomless" void—the absolute source of all things before any light, dark, or creation existed.</note>, and is its own foundation, can operate entirely within itself; for this is its own essence, it acts upon itself.

2. Although the soul is a branch proceeding from the trunk, it has nevertheless been brought into being as a creature, and it belongs to itself. Now, it is an image of the universal <note>The "universal" here refers to the macrocosm—the entirety of the divine and natural worlds. Böhme views the soul as a microcosm, containing the same structures as the whole universe.</note>, and it is a child of the universal. For when the child is born, the mother and the child are distinct; they make two persons. But as long as it is still within the seed of the mother, it is the mother's seed, and the mother governs it.

3. For once the child is born, it has its own life within itself; it possesses the center of life within its own power. It governs not only within itself, but outside of itself, in that which is seed.

4. Therefore, understand us well. The Spirit of God and the spirit of the soul are two persons; each is independent of the other, and yet both are in the first beginning; each of them has its own will.

<summary>Böhme explains that while the soul originates from God (the "trunk"), it becomes a distinct, self-governing entity or "person" upon its creation. This autonomy grants the soul its own power and free will, mirroring the creative capacity of the divine abyss.</summary>
<keywords>Unground, abyss, free will, microcosm, macrocosm, Spirit of God, soul's power, autonomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Sixth Question regarding the power of the soul. It focuses on the relationship between the soul and the Holy Spirit as its creator, and the necessity of keeping spiritual secrets from the ungodly.</meta>

109
### Forty Questions. 6th Question:

5. Now, it is right that the child be obedient to the father, under penalty of disinheritance <term>exhérédation: the legal act of depriving an heir of their inheritance</term>. The Holy Spirit was the maker of the soul, and he created it; he has the right to demand obedience from the spirit of the soul, under penalty of losing the inheritance of the Holy Spirit, or of the Divinity.

6. And although there would be much to write here, it would nevertheless be dangerous, because of false magic. For what the false spirit knows, it uses to the advantage of sorcery <note>Böhme frequently warns against revealing too much spiritual knowledge because it might be misused by those seeking power through magic or occult practices rather than divine love.</note>.

---

7. However, we wish to write in such a way that the children <note>Referring to the "children of Light" or spiritual initiates.</note> may understand us, but without recklessly surrendering everything to them. For it is not good to write [everything], as one does not know who the reader will be.

8. As for the impious, we tell them that they belong to the demon, and that they must have no part in our writings. We enclose them behind a wall and within a thick barrier, so that they may be blind and not know our spirit; for we do not wish to place the serpent there. Our will has separated itself from them; that is why they must not know us, and even if they held us in their hand, there would be a powerful seal upon our writings for them.

### Forty Questions. 6th Question.

27. This is why we are the children of the Almighty God and the heirs of His treasures in omnipotence.

## SEVENTH QUESTION.

->*Whether the soul is corporeal or incorporeal?*<-

1. A thing that does not proceed from any beginning also has nothing in itself that could give it anything; and if, however, it does possess something, it seeks the beginning of it within itself, for every spirit dwells in the deepest abyss of its essence. But if it is to work its own substance <term>substance: in the philosophy of Jacob Böhme, this refers to the spiritual "body" or manifestation that an essence creates for itself</term>, then it must not inhabit anything foreign, but rather dwell in itself, in its own essence.

2. When God created the soul, the Holy Spirit clothed it with the tincture <term>tincture: a vital spiritual essence or "color" that Böhme describes as the bridge between spirit and matter, giving life and quality to a being</term>; for it is in this tincture that the soul partly consists. It was naked in itself, just as red fire is naked, and it was clothed with the tincture, just as you understand that vegetation results from heat—which is but an impulse of the tincture, causing branches to emerge from the root or from their own fire, whether that fire be cold or hot.

3. For the cold fire is held within the darkness until anguish <note>original: "l'angoisse"; in Böhme’s system, "anguish" (Angst) refers to the intense, contracting tension of the spiritual qualities as they struggle to reach the light</note> has reached it. Then it ignites into heat, as you can see in a plant when it rises to a new property <term>property: a specific quality, power, or characteristic of a spiritual being</term>.

4. The tincture is the true body of the soul. For the soul is fire; and from the fire proceeds the tincture, which in turn draws the fire back into itself. It is through this that the fire is tempered, so that its wrathful source <note>original: "source colérique"; in Böhme’s system, this refers to the "gall" or the harsh, bitter, and burning quality of the first principles of nature before they are transformed by the Light</note> is extinguished.

5. Thus the tincture subsists in sweetness, for it has within itself no substance of power; rather, the fire is its power, which becomes water through the sweetness of the tincture. For fire is desiring; and where the desire of the origin exists, there also is found the discovery of the origin.

6. Thus the fire finds the water in the tincture, and it changes it into sulfur <note>original: "soufre"; here representing a specific alchemical stage of manifestation where the spirit begins to take on a more defined, albeit still spiritual, form</note>, through the power of the seven spirits of nature <term>seven spirits of nature: the seven fundamental qualities or "Source-Spirits" that Böhme describes as the building blocks of both the divine and material worlds</term>. This is a water of life. For the tincture causes growth to emerge in the water like a plant, and it is the fire in the abyss (the darkness) that is the cause of it.

7. Thus in the mystery, the water is changed into the sulfur of the seven spirits. For the great arcane <term>arcane: from the Latin 'arcanum,' meaning a profound secret or a hidden mystery of nature and divinity</term> of what God and eternity are capable of is hidden within.

8. Thus the mystery contains two forms, which are fire and water, and it modifies itself according to both; namely, into red, according to the fire, and into white, according to the water; by this means, there results from the fire a radiance, or a clarity, which allows life to see and know itself. It is from this that reason and thoughts proceed, and the soul is in the wheel of anguish <term>wheel of anguish: also known as the Wheel of Nature, this describes the restless, revolving tension of the soul's inner qualities as they seek the light</term>, in the fire, from which the essences are produced.

9. You see by this what the blood is; it is

2. In our third book, we have written about its propagation <note>The process by which life is passed from one generation to the next.</note> deeply, extensively, and with many details. He possessed the tincture <term>tincture: in Böhme’s mystical chemistry, the spiritualizing essence or "inner quality" that gives life and form to matter.</term> of fire and of water, that is to say, the soul and the spirit; and he was meant, through his imagination <note>For Böhme, "imagination" is the creative power of the will to give form to spiritual reality.</note> and his own love, to beget from himself his likeness, or an image according to himself; he was also meant to perform this work without tearing <note>A reference to Böhme’s belief that original reproduction would have been a painless, spiritual projection rather than the physical "tearing" of birth.</note>.

3. For, as it has been explained above, just as the soul has enough power to change the body into another form, so too would it have had the power to produce from itself a branch homogeneous to its own property, if Adam had withstood the trial.

4. But as he imagined into the universal power, and allowed the spirit of this world and the serpent to enter into the soul, into the tincture; and as he allowed himself to be dazzled by the earthly fruit to the point of eating of good and evil, then his tincture conceived an analogous image, or a monster that is half earthly. Furthermore, the *turba* <term>turba: a Latin term used by Böhme to describe "turmoil" or "disruption"—the destructive force that enters when divine harmony is broken.</term> immediately insinuated itself into it and sought the limit.

5. Thus the noble image found itself within the earthly, and then destruction and death began, and Adam no longer had the power to beget, and his omnipotence was lost; and it would have been lost forever, if the heart of God had not immediately surrounded itself with the word of the pro- <note>The text likely intended "promise" or "prophecy," referring to the divine plan for humanity's eventual redemption.</note>

<summary>Böhme explains that Adam was originally a genderless being who was intended to reproduce spiritually through his own "tincture" and "imagination" without physical pain. The Fall occurred when Adam turned his focus toward the material world, leading to the loss of his divine power and the introduction of death and the "turba" (turmoil) into the human condition.</summary>

## QUESTION TENTH.

*Whether the soul is propagated by transmission, and in the human bodily manner, or else if each time it is created anew, and breathed in by God.*

1. I do not understand the intelligence and philosophy of the world, since it cannot resolve this question. However, I have no intention of blaming you for this: for I know that these matters are debated among the learned in the schools, where they nevertheless never cease to argue. But I marvel at their proud blindness, and that their reason has no knowledge of God.

2. Consider here, you wise ones, what you are, or what you understand of the mystery of God? Absolutely nothing, and yet you wish to teach. You would do much better to carry a shepherd’s crook <note>original: "houlette de berger" — a traditional staff used by shepherds, symbolizing a humble life of manual labor.</note> in your hand than to clothe yourselves in the habit of Christ <note>Refers to the clerical robes and the professional status of theologians and priests who claim spiritual authority.</note>.

## QUESTION ELEVENTH.

->*In what manner and in what place is the seat of the soul found in man?*<-

1. A thing which is unfathomable <note>original: "insondable"—this refers to the *Ungrund*, Böhme's concept of the "groundless" or "abyss," the absolute nothingness and everything that precedes God’s self-manifestation.</note>, and which nevertheless seeks and works within itself for a foundation, can only have its origin and its seat in the first compaction <term>compaction: the spiritual process where the formless will "thickens" or gathers itself into a specific point or focus of existence.</term>, there where it compacts within itself, and where the limit is; that is to say, in the deepest part of all interiors. It is from there that it emerges from itself and seeks before itself; thus it successively produces one mirror <term>mirror: in Böhme's thought, a reflection or "speculum" through which the soul or the divine can perceive its own image and hidden nature.</term> upon the model of another, until it finds again the first or unfathomable limit. Such also is the soul’s way of being.

# TWELFTH QUESTION.

## How does the soul become enlightened?

1. We must observe that if the sun were taken away from this world, everything would be in darkness. Then external reason would say: we are in dark death and in the harshness of cold, and indeed this would be so.

2. Now, look, dear soul, consider that when your body breaks apart, your spirit then loses the subtle <term>subtle: likely referring to the "subtle body" or the refined material interface (spiritus mundi) that allows the soul to interact with the physical world</term>. How then do you expect to be in the light? and with what do you intend to see? We present this with simplicity to your mind, so that you may reflect upon it.

3. There is no darkness for a thing that is in eternal liberty, and which continually enters into liberty, for it dwells in nothing that could bring it darkness. It is free like the eye of God, which sees into itself through substance <term>substance: in Böhme’s thought, this is "divine corporality" or the spiritual "flesh" of God, rather than gross matter</term>.

4. If it imagines <note>original: "imagine." In Böhmean terminology, to "imagine" is to create or form oneself into a state through the power of the will and desire.</note> [itself] into the attraction for something, then the will goes into that "something" which the desiring attraction itself produces. This same "something" takes the will into itself and overshadows it in such a way that it remains in darkness, and can have no light, unless it

## FOURTEENTH QUESTION.

->*Whether a new soul of this kind is without sin?*<-

1. We understand here the soul propagated in a newborn child. My dear friend, this is a very arduous question. But I must not leave you without an answer, for the time of the manifestation <note>The "time of manifestation" refers to a period Böhme believed had begun, where the hidden mysteries of God and nature were being revealed to humanity.</note> is born. The day is dawning, the night is in flight; therefore, let thanks and praise be given to God, who has begotten us anew for the light, and for an inheritance that will never fade, and has adopted us as his beloved children.

2. My dear friend, you know well the terrible fault of Adam, just as we have amply set it forth in all our writings; namely, that the soul turned its right eye <note>Böhme frequently uses the metaphor of the "two eyes" of the soul: the right eye gazes into eternity and God, while the left eye gazes into time and the world.</note> away from God and into the spirit of this world, and became disobedient toward God; that it lost its <term>noble image<note>The "noble image" is the original divine likeness or "Sophia" that humanity possessed before the Fall.</note></term>, and substituted for it a monstrous image, and gave itself over to the spirit of this world; whereas by its will, it should have powerfully dominated over it, and as a soul, never eaten of good and evil.

3. Now, it has nonetheless transgressed the commandment of God, and has placed its <term>imagination<note>In Böhme's system, "imagination" is a technical term for the creative power of the soul's desire, which "images" or gives form to spiritual substance.</note></term> into the sp—

## FIFTEENTH QUESTION.

->*How does sin enter into the soul, if it is the work and creation of God?*<-

1. This is how—as has been explained above—the *turba* and the earthly attraction come together into this world, and the soul is now strongly pulled in two directions; namely, first, by the Word of the Lord <note>original: *le Verbe du Seigneur*; referring to the Divine Logos or Christ as the creative and redeeming principle.</note> who has intervened in the middle, who there, through love, became man; who draws the soul continually into the kingdom of God and reveals the *turba* to the soul's eyes; so that the soul sees in nature what is false and what is sin; and if it allows itself to be drawn, it is <term>regenerated</term> <note>original: *régénérée*; the process of spiritual rebirth where the soul is restored to its original divine image.</note> in the Word, until it becomes the image of God.

2. Secondly, the *turba* also draws the soul powerfully into its alliance and constantly communicates the earthly attraction to it, “particularly in youth, where the earthly tree breaks through, full of budding essences and stinging poisons; it is also then that the *turba* insinuates itself powerful-”

3. A thing that comes from two beginnings, and is of equal weight, soon tips to one side, whether toward evil or toward good.

4. Sin does not create itself, but it is the will that carries it out. It enters the spirit through <term>imagination</term> <note>original: *l'imagination*; here, Böhme uses the term to describe the "forming" power of the mind—the act of focusing the soul's desire on an object until it takes shape within the spirit.</note>; for the spirit enters into a thing and becomes infected by that thing; then the <term>turba</term> <note>original: *turba*; a Latin term meaning "turmoil" or "uproar." 5. Thus, anything that desires to introduce the external into the will is a sin. The will should only strive toward love and sweetness <note>original: *douceur*; often translated as "meekness" in mystical texts, representing the gentle, light-filled nature of the divine.</note>, as if it were nothing or as if it were dead. It must desire nothing but the life of God—that life which God has created within it. Furthermore, in everything the soul does, its will must be directed in such a way that it is for God that it acts; for if it places its will within the "thing" itself, it then introduces that thing into the spirit, such that it takes possession of its heart. In this way, the *turba* is fathered, and the soul is imprisoned by the thing.

# SEVENTEENTH QUESTION.

---

## *What is the origin and the reason for the opposition that exists between the spirit and the flesh?*

---

1. My dear sir and brother, you well know that there is an enmity between fire and water, for fire is life; thus water is its death; which you see clearly when one throws water into the fire: then the source of fire is repelled, and the fire is in death.

2. But in man (this fire) is not entirely in death, because of the light that the fire promotes unceasingly, and yet there is an enmity, just as there is an enmity between God and Hell; and nevertheless Hell, or the fire of wrath (and not the demon as a demon), is of God <note>The author argues that the "fire of wrath" is a foundational part of the divine order, serving as the "dark" or "strenuous" ground from which the light of God's love emerges.</note>.

### *How does the soul separate from the body in man at death?*

<meta>The text from this heading until the end of the page was underlined in red ink by a later hand in the original manuscript.</meta>

1. ->*How the soul is mortal, and how it is immortal?*<-

1. A thing that has an eternal beginning also has an eternal end; such is the essence of the soul <note>Böhme suggests that because the soul originates from the eternal "Unground" or the nature of God, its "end" is not a disappearance, but a return to that same eternal state.</note>.

## QUESTION TWENTY-TWO.

->What does each soul do, and does it rejoice until the day of the last judgment?<-

1. This question reaches the glorious gate of the kingdom of joy, where the <term>triumphant crown of the soul: a symbol of the soul’s spiritual victory and its ultimate state of glory in the presence of the Divine</term> is recognized.

2. When a beloved child travels into foreign and distant lands to acquire <note>original: "sciences" — used here in the older sense of comprehensive knowledge, wisdom, or learning</note> knowledge and honor, they often think of their home and the time when they will rejoice with their parents and friends. They are delighted at the thought of that day; they await it with a secret joy and with longing; and at the same time, they apply themselves to their purpose, in order to gather a store of knowledge and learning that can bring satisfaction to their whole family, and to all those whom they love.

3. You may apply this comparison to the soul, and we ask you to observe that souls without the body have a great inner joy, and that they await with an ardent, secret desire the <term>last judgment: in this context, the final restoration where the spiritual and physical worlds are fully reconciled</term> where they are to receive once again their beautiful and holy <note>garment: likely referring to the "spiritual body" or "heavenly corporeality" that Böhme believes the soul regains at the end of time</note> garment, accompanied by wonders. Thus their magnificence is in their will, in which, according to the manner of the eter- <note>The text breaks mid-word at the end of the page; "éter-" almost certainly completes as "éternité" (eternity).</note>

It is then indeed that one would see a great number of people who would withdraw from Sodom, from Gomorrah, from <term>Babel</term><note>Böhme uses "Babel" to symbolize the world of spiritual confusion, hypocrisy, and false religious institutions.</note>, and from the lamentable valley of greed and pride, which is nothing but anguish and torment, and which is filled only with restlessness, pain, and terror.

17. Their expectation is similar to that of a prisoner who, as soon as something moves, always listens to hear if it is not the executioner arriving to carry out the judgment, and to pay him as he deserves. This is their situation.

## TWENTY-THIRD QUESTION.

1. A thing that moves within the eternal beginning is also in the eternal end. Who is it that will give something to one who is far away, and is not in a place where one can give to them? ## QUESTION TWENTY-FOUR.

*Whether the prayers of mortals will bring any profit to these souls, and whether or not they make any impression upon them.*

->•<-

1. My dear friend, consider here the souls of the rich man and the poor Lazarus <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 16:19–31, where a "great gulf" is fixed between the rich man in torment and Lazarus in the afterlife, preventing passage from one side to the other.</note>; you will see that there is a great separation between them and us, and that those who, through their prayers and their will, strive to go from here to them, cannot do so, just as they cannot come to us; there is a principle <term>principle: In Böhme's philosophy, a "principle" (French: principe) refers to one of the three fundamental realms of existence: the dark fire-world (the Father's wrath), the light world (the Son's love), or the external material world. These realms are distinct "dimensions" that do not physically touch.</term> in the interval.

2. The prayers and intercessions of the righteous penetrate into heaven, and not into hell. Therefore, the Scripture says: that for hell there is no deliverance. The souls are in hell like the bones of the dead <note>This likely refers to Psalm 141:7, suggesting a state of spiritual desolation and dryness where life has completely departed.</note>. They call out, but no one hears them. There are no prayers that are useful to them; and even if many men were to pray for the damned souls, nevertheless their prayers would remain within their own principle; they would go into heaven and not into hell. There is no recall from hell, says Christ.

### *What is the hand of God, and the bosom of Abraham?*

1. This has been sufficiently explained: for it is the universal presence of God, but within his <term>principle: Böhme often uses "principle" to describe one of the fundamental states of existence—light/heaven, dark/wrath, or the physical world.</term>. ## TWENTY-SIXTH QUESTION.

*Whether the souls of the dead concern themselves with men, children, friends, and their possessions; and whether they know, see, approve, or disapprove of their occupations.*

1. My dear friend, this question is beyond human understanding and knowledge according to external reason. <note>original: "raison externe." ## TWENTY-EIGHTH QUESTION.

*Whether the soul has greater knowledge of divine, angelic, earthly, and even demonic things than when it was in its body, and whether it can experience and judge them with more certainty.*

1. As for divine and angelic knowledge, the soul truly has much more of it, for it exists within the <term>principle</term> <note>The "principle" refers to the fundamental source or spiritual foundation of God's being.</note> of God. Just as a son sees everything the father does in the house, so the soul sees what is in heaven. The knowledge of these souls is not equal, however: for the highest lights shine only in <term>majesty</term> <note>The "light of majesty" is Böhme’s term for the full, glorious manifestation of God's presence, as opposed to his hidden or wrathful aspects.</note>; and this is why most souls are obliged to wait until the final judgment, when they will recover their new body.

2. But the holy souls who are eminently enlightened, who exist within the body and the <term>virtuality</term> <note>original: *virtualité*. These are the *Magnalia*, the great works or manifestations of God's power and creativity.</note> of God, while they wait for their own wonders to be represented to them.

But there will be no jealous animosity; rather, each will rejoice in the beauty of the other, since there is no other light there but God, who fills all in all.

3. For all the prophets speak of the *turba*. They uncover that which is false, and they declare what would be better, and what enters into the will of God.

# FORTIETH QUESTION.

->*Whether paradise shall pass away, and what shall exist afterward?*<-

1. Paradise is no more transient than God, for it is a portion of the Divinity. When the external regime <note>original: *régime extérieur*, referring to the current material world order and physical laws governed by time and decay</note> has passed away, there will be a true paradise in the place where the world is now.

2. For there will be an earth proceeding from celestial substantiality <term>celestial substantiality: In Böhme's theosophy, this refers to "heavenly corporality"—a pure, spiritual substance that is the true "flesh" of the divine realm, unlike the heavy matter of our current world</term>, which we will be able to inhabit in every aspect of its capacity. On the last day, we shall not rise up above the location of this world, but we shall remain thus in *our native land*, and we shall enter into our dwelling in another world, in another principle <term>principle: (*principe*) A fundamental realm of existence; Böhme describes three "principles"—the dark fire-world, the light world (Paradise), and the external material world</term> which will have another source.

3. For there will no longer be frost, nor heat, nor night, and we will be able to penetrate everywhere through the celestial earth, without causing any breakage <note>This implies a glorified state where the body can move through spiritual matter without physical resistance.</note>.

4. This earth will be like a sea of glass <note>A reference to Revelation 4:6, describing the crystalline transparency of the divine realm.</note>, and transparent, through which all the wonders of the world will be seen very clearly, because the splendor of God will be its light;

<summary>This page describes the transition of the physical world into an eternal, transparent "celestial earth" where Paradise becomes fully manifest. # CONCLUSION.

THUS, my cherished friend, we have given you a precise answer to your question, according to our gift; and we fraternally warn you not to despise us because of our simple language and our little skill; for we are not engendered by art <note>here meaning human artifice, academic rhetoric, or formal scholarship</note>, but by simplicity, and we speak of high things with common words. ### *The Reverse Eye, which treats of the soul and its image, and furthermore of the turba which destroys the image.*
<note>The "Reverse Eye" (L'œil retourné) refers to the mystical concept of the soul turning its gaze inward or back toward its divine source. "Turba" is a technical term used by Böhme to describe a state of spiritual disturbance, turmoil, or the "awakened wrath" that disrupts divine harmony.</note>

1. The **soul** is an eye (plunging) into the eternal abyss. It is a likeness of eternity, a complete figure and an image in conformity with the first principle, and similar to God the Father according to His person and according to eternal nature; its essence and its substantiality (considering it purely and only in itself) is primarily the wheel of nature <term>wheel of nature: in Böhmean cosmology, this refers to the "Seven Properties" or the dynamic cycle of forces that bring life and form out of the divine abyss</term> with the first four forms.

2. For the word of the Lord shaped the soul by means of the eternal *fiat* <note>Latin: "let it be done"; refers to the creative command of God</note>, in the eternal will of the Father, in the center of eternal nature, and manifested it through the Holy Spirit, or breathed it in like a fire that is hidden in eternity, in which all the forms of eternal nature have existed from all eternity, and have only been known eternally in the wisdom of God, in divine magic <term>magie divine: the spiritual power of the divine will to create and manifest wonders</term>, as a figure or an image without substantiality.

# C O N C L U S I O N.

**THUS**, my dear friend, we have given you a precise response to your question, according to our gift; and we fraternally warn you not to despise us because of our simple language, and our lack of skill; for we are not begotten by art <note>The author uses "art" to mean formal academic training or human artifice</note>, but by simplicity, and we speak of high things with common words. Take them as a gift from God, and you will find there great things that you will not encounter among the most distinguished, clever orators in their art, unless they too are begotten of this same school. # ON THE SUBLIME AND DEEP FOUNDATION

## OF THE SIX POINTS.

I. On the <term>vegetation</term><note>In this mystical context, "vegetation" refers to the organic, spiritual unfolding or growth of divine and natural forces, rather than just plant life.</note> of the <term>three principles</term><note>A core concept in Böhme’s philosophy representing three realms: the dark fire-source (First Principle), the light of divine love (Second Principle), and the external visible world (Third Principle).</note>; what each is in itself, and how it begets itself into a "tree" or a "life." How one must seek and recognize the foundation of nature.

II. On the mixed tree of good and evil, or the life of the three principles one within the other; how it unites and accords with itself.

III. On the origin of the opposition (or contrariety) of <term>vegetation</term>, in which life in itself is in conflict.

IV. How the holy and good tree of eternal life grows from, and through, all the <term>vegetations</term> of the three principles, and is grasped by none of them.

V. On the tree and the <term>vegetation</term> of the life of perdition; how a life becomes corrupted—that is, how it passes from a source of love and joy into a source of suffering which is contrary to all other lives.

VI. On the life of darkness in which the demons dwell; what generation and what source it has.

# PREFACE

## TO THE READER

---

We have not written this work at all for the unreasoning animals who, on the outside, have the form of man, but who in their inner image and spirit are wicked and wild beasts—a state which manifests and reveals itself in their inherent qualities. Rather, we have written for those who are images of men: for those who emerge from a <term>beastly image</term> <note>The author refers to a state of being driven by base instincts rather than spiritual reason</note> into the image of a human being; who belong to the Kingdom of God, and who sincerely desire to live and grow in the image of man—in the <term>true man</term> <note>original: "vrai homme", a reference to the perfected spiritual state of humanity</note>. These are individuals who are often and forcefully held back by an opposing way of life, and are thus placed in a <term>mixed life</term> <note>A state of existence characterized by the ongoing struggle between spiritual aspirations and earthly, material burdens</note>, and who labor for the generation of a holy life. It is for these people that we have produced this writing, and we tell them not to consider it impossible to recognize and to know such <term>secrets</term>; and we...

<summary>In this preface, the author defines his intended audience: not those living by animalistic instincts, but seekers struggling to transcend their lower nature to achieve a "true" spiritual humanity. He encourages these readers to believe that divine secrets are attainable despite the difficulties of a life caught between two worlds.</summary>
<keywords>true man, mixed life, spiritual transformation, beastly image, Kingdom of God, divine secrets, human nature</keywords>

# THE THIRD POINT.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*On the origin of the opposition of plants, in which life is in conflict within itself.*<-

1. A thing that is one, which has only one will <term>will</term> <note>original: "volonté." In this philosophy, the "will" is the driving force of all existence, from the lowest plant to the highest spirit.</note>, does not struggle against itself. But when there are several wills in a single thing, it then becomes a site of conflict, for each will wishes to follow its own determined path. However, if one is the mistress of the others, and has complete power over them all, such that she may break them if they are not submissive to her, then the multiplicity of the thing consists of a single substance <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substance." This refers to the essential nature or "stuff" that makes up a being or object.</note>; for the plurality of wills all submit in obedience to their sovereign.

<summary>This page concludes the warning against demonic envy and introduces the "Third Point," which explores how multiple competing wills within a single substance create conflict unless they are governed by a sovereign power.</summary>

2. Thus, we give you to understand the opposition within life, for life consists of several wills <term>wills</term> <note>original: "volontés." In this mystical context, "will" refers to the inherent drive or directional force of any natural quality.</note>. Each essence can produce a will, and indeed does so. For the astringent, the bitter, the anxious <note>original: "angoisseux." In this way, fire is the enemy of all the others, for it places every source into great anguish, such that there is a great opposition between them. There, each combats the other, as can be seen in heat and cold, fire and water, life and death.

3. Similarly, the life of man combats itself. Each form combats the other, not only in man but in all creatures, unless the forms of life receive a gentle and lovable sovereign, under whose constraint they are placed, and who can break their power and their will. It is the light of life that is the sovereign of all forms, and which can contain them all; they must all surrender their will to the light, and they do so willingly, for the light gives them sweetness and power, so that their forms—whether astringent, strong, bitter, or anxious—are all changed into loveliness. They all give their will to the light of life, and the light gives them sweetness <term>sweetness</term> <note>original: "douceur." A technical term in Boehme's philosophy representing the harmonizing influence of divine Love that transforms the "wrathful" qualities of nature.</note>.

# THE IV. POINT.

## CHAPTER V.

*How the holy and good tree of eternal life grows from the <term>vegetation</term> <note>In this mystical context, "vegetation" refers to the "growing power" or the "vital force" that drives the development of spiritual and natural life.</note>, and through the vegetation of all the <term>three principles</term> <note>A central concept in Böhme’s philosophy: the three "worlds" or "realms" consisting of the dark fire-world (the Father), the light-world (the Son), and the outward, visible world (the Holy Spirit/Nature).</note>, and is grasped by none.*

...a base; for the dark world <term>dark world: In Böhme’s thought, the "dark world" (*Finsterniswelt*) is not "evil" in a simple sense, but represents the raw, fiery, and foundational energy of nature before it is illuminated by light.</term> is the foundation of nature, and the eternal unfathomable will, which is named the Father, is the foundation of the dark world as has been stated above; and the world of light is hidden within the dark world, and the dark world is also hidden within the world of light.

But if he encounters a struggle within himself, such that his inner will <term>inner will: the core spiritual intent of a person, often contrasted with the "external" or "fleshly" desires</term> fights always and at every moment against these evil properties, exterminates them, and does not let them manifest into an evil substance; so that he always wishes to do good, and yet finds that these evil properties hold him back; so that he cannot always put into practice what he would wish, and yet finds the desire for amendment and penitence <note>original: "pénitence," referring here to a state of humble repentance and turning back toward God</note>; so that a permanent desire for divine mercy wells up within him, in such a way that he would truly do good if only he could.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*On the true human essence (proceeding) from the essence of God.*<-

1. **The** true positive human essence <term>essence: (French: "essence", German: "Wesenheit") refers to the actual spiritual substance or "stuff" of the soul, rather than just an abstract concept</term> is not earthly, nor of the dark world; it is simply born in the world of light; it has no communication with the darkness, nor with the external world; there is between them a great barrier, namely, death <note>Böhme often describes "death" as the boundary or "gulf" between different spiritual dimensions or "worlds."</note>.

For it brings to both nothing but the power for perdition. For as soon as God’s covenant is declared, it never passes away without fruit. God operates in His covenant according to His word.

29. As the soul is that declares the covenant, so also is the medicine within the covenant; and it is in a similar power that the spirit of God operates in love and wrath; for He is the spirit of all life, and accords with all lives. He is in each thing according to the will and the property <term>property: (French: *propriété*) A technical term in Böhme’s theosophy referring to the inherent quality, character, or "signature" of a being that dictates how it reacts to divine influence.</term> of that thing. For one property seizes the other. What the soul wills, He wills also; there, it turns itself inward.

30. What the will of a thing desires, it receives. A toad takes into itself nothing but poison, even if it were to enter into the best pharmacies <note>original: *pharmacies*; in the 17th-century context, this refers to an apothecary shop filled with healing herbs and substances.</note>; it is the same with a serpent. Each thing takes into itself only its own property, even if it were to eat the substance of a good property; nevertheless, it converts everything within itself into its own property. Even if a toad were to eat honey, it would nevertheless become—

# THE VI. POINT.

## CHAPTER IX.

*Of the life of darkness, in which the demons dwell; what generation or source it has.*

1. The life of darkness is, in all lives, the opposite of the light. For the darkness gives a wrathful <term>wrathful essence: (French: *essence colérique*) In theosophical terms, this refers to a harsh, "fiery" state of being characterized by conflict and agitation, lacking the cooling "water" of divine love.</term> and hostile essence; and the life of light gives the essence of love.

2. In the darkness, there is within the essences nothing but a continual stinging and shattering. There, each form of the essences combats the others as an opposing essence. Each form denies itself, and each says to the other that it is evil, and its opposite, that it is a cause of its trouble and of its wrathful state. Each one thinks: "If only the other form did not exist, you would have rest." However, both are evil and false. From this it comes that everything generated from the dark, wrathful property <term>property: (French: *propriété*) The specific quality or internal disposition that defines a being's nature.</term> is a liar, and denies the other forms as being evil, and yet—

### CHAPTER X.

*On the four elements of the demon and of the dark world; how one can recognize them in this external world.*

1. The first element of the dark world and of the demon is pride; the second is greed; the third is envy; the fourth is wrath. These four elements always and eternally beget a young son called falsehood. This same son is a true child of the lost Adam <note>Referring to the fallen state of humanity after the biblical original sin.</note>, whom he has left behind as sovereign of the world, who has become king in the world, and has possessed the whole world, and governs in all respects within the third principle <note>In Boehme’s cosmology, the "Third Principle" is the visible, material universe we inhabit, which sits between the realms of light and darkness.</note>. He who knows this king well, knows the four elements of the demon; for in the dark world, these four elements have complete dominion, in spirit and in body, and are called the substance in all things.

2. And we see clearly in this, that this external world rests upon the foundation of these same four elements, and receives from them its inclination, as well as its source and will; for the son of these same four elements <note>Falsehood, as identified in the previous paragraph.</note> reigns upon the earth, and wishes to have everything under his obedience and has four families for—

## A SHORT EXPLANATION OF THE FOLLOWING SIX POINTS.

I. *Of the blood and the water of the soul.*
II. *Of predestination. Of good and evil.*
III. *Of sin. What sin is; and how it is a sin.*
IV. *How Christ delivered His kingdom to His Father.*
V. *Of magic. What magic is; and what the magical foundation is.*
VI. *Of the mystery; what it is.*

---

### THE FIRST POINT.

->*Of the blood and the water of the soul.*<-

1. Everything that is substantial and graspable exists in this world. Now, since the soul has no substance or being in this world, its blood and its water likewise have no substance or being in this world.

2. In truth, the soul exists with its blood and its water within the external blood and water; but its substance is <term>magical</term> <note>original: "magique." In the context of theosophy, "magic" refers to the spiritual power of the will that gives form to reality, rather than sorcery or superstition.</note>. For the soul is also a <term>magical fire</term> <note>A term used to describe the soul as a dynamic, energetic force of desire and will that "burns" with spiritual life.</note>,

2. and its image or its form is generated in the light (in the power of its fire and its light), and is nevertheless a true image in flesh and blood, but understanding it in the same manner <note>That is, understanding "flesh and blood" in a spiritual or "magical" sense rather than a physical, earthly sense.</note>.

3. Just as the wisdom of God possesses <term>essence</term> <note>original: "l'essence." In this context, it refers to spiritual substantiality or the "beingness" that allows a spirit to have a form.</note>, and yet wisdom itself is not the essence, so also the soul with its image possesses essence, and yet the soul is only a <term>magical fire</term>, while its nourishment is drawn from its essence.

5. For it gives color to everything, and in its form it passes from divine <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "vertu." Here meaning "power" or "potency" rather than moral rectitude.</note> into the sweet essence of the light—understand this according to the property of the light; and it is an agent of <term>transmutation</term> <note>The process of changing one state of being into a higher, more spiritual one.</note> according to the property of the fire; it can lead everything into its highest degree, though it is not a living spirit, but the highest being.

6. Thus there is a similar being in the water, and it conducts therein the property of the fire and the light, along with all the virtues of nature; for there it changes the water into blood; it performs this as much in the external and internal water as in the external and internal fire.

### II.

### *On Predestination. Concerning Good and Evil.*

1. GOD from all eternity is alone "all." His essence is divided into three eternal distinctions. One is the world of fire; the second is the world of *darkness*, and the third is the world of light.

### III.

->*Of sin. What sin is, and how sin exists.*<-

1. A thing that is one has neither commandment nor law. But if it mingles with another, then there are two beings in one, and there are also two wills. There, one runs against the other, and there an enmity arises.

2. Thus we must reflect upon the enmity against God. God is alone and good, apart from all sources <note>original: "sources." In Böhme's cosmology, these are the *Quellgeister* or "fountain-spirits"—the fundamental forces (like contraction, friction, and heat) that produce the "fire" of existence.</note>; and although all the sources are in him, nevertheless they are not manifest; for the good has swallowed the evil or the opposition into itself, and holds it by force within the good, like a prisoner. There, the evil must be a cause of life and light, but not manifest. But the good stifles the evil, so that it <note>The "it" refers to the divine life.</note> may live in itself within the evil, without torment or sensibility. <note>Böhme argues that the "dark" qualities are the necessary friction that generates the "light" of life, but in a state of grace, that friction is not felt as pain.</note>

3. Love and enmity are but a single thing, but each remains in itself; that makes two things. Death is the boundary of separation between them, and yet there is no death, except that the good dies to the evil, just as light is dead to the torment of the fire, and no longer feels the fire.

### V.

#### *On Magic. What Magic Is. What the Magical Foundation Is.*

1. Magic is the mother of eternity, of the essence of all essences, for it makes itself, and is understood <note>original: "entendue." In this context, Böhme implies that magic is perceived or realized through the faculty of desire.</note> in desire.

2. It is nothing in itself but a will; and this same will is the great mystery <note>original: "grand mystère." This corresponds to the *Mysterium Magnum*, a central term in Böhme’s philosophy referring to the primordial "chaos" or "abyss" from which God brings forth all creation.</note> of all wonders and all secrets, and carries itself into substance through the imagination of the desiring hunger.

3. It is the origin of nature. Its desire creates a figuration <note>original: "figuration." The process by which the formless will takes on a specific shape or "image" within the mind or the spirit.</note>. The figuration is only the will of the desire; but the desire creates, within the will, a being similar to what the will is in itself.

4. True magic is not any being <note>original: "aucun être." It is not a thing or a creature, but the *process* of becoming.</note>, but the spirit desiring being; it is an insubstantial matrix, and it manifests itself in being.

5. Magic is spirit, and being is its body, and yet the two are but one; just as the body and the soul are but one single person.

6. Magic is the most secret thing, for it is above nature. It creates nature according to the form of its will; it is the mystery of the Ternary <note>original: "Trinaire." Referring to the Trinity, but specifically how the three persons of the Godhead interact to produce the act of creation.</note>: understand the will within the desire for the heart of God,

Now think about what you are doing, for <term>Babel</term> <note>Babel represents the world of spiritual confusion and corrupt human institutions that are destined for destruction.</note> is already in flames, and it burns; there is nothing more to extinguish it, nor any remedy. It has been recognized as evil; its reign is coming to an end, etc. *Hallelujah* <note>original: "Alleluia"</note>.
